“I confess that I am only formed to move along the ground,” the horse continued, “But how graceful is my make! How well turned my limbs! How highly finished my whole body! How great my strength! The F-22 is the US air supremacy fighter, the F-35 is a fighterbomber. It is designed to engage air to air, but also to be configurable for multiple missions.

Also the article linked in the blog even says:

"The reasonable conclusion of all this: the F-35 is not a top dogfighting aircraft because it wasn’t designed to be one. And it wasn’t designed to be one because it is better to kill the enemy from a distance before the enemy can target you."

The F-22 was procured in much smaller numbers than was planned, due to high cost. The F-35 was intended to supplement it as an air-superiority fighter. It's also supposed to replace the F-16, and the F-15, and the F-18, and the A-10, and the Growler, and other platforms.

"The reasonable conclusion of all this: the F-35 is not a top dogfighting aircraft because it wasn’t designed to be one. And it wasn’t designed to be one because it is better to kill the enemy from a distance before the enemy can target you."

That's some backward-ass reasoning. "It can't do it so it wasn't designed to do it". It's also, unsurprisingly, wrong. In any case, the fact that it will be asked to take on roles for which it "wasn't designed" should speak volumes.

Also, the whole "kill them from a distance before they target you" isn't as simple as that in real life because your enemy is also going to be stealthy, use long range missiles, use passive sensors and use countermeasures. The use of passive sensors against an IR-stealthy enemy will reduce engagement distances a great deal. And the enemy will also have countermeasures, just like the F-35 does. All of this means the two forces may well come to a merge, which means dogfighting, which means the F-35 gets its ass kicked. Also, even if the engagement happens at long distance, the F-35's lack of agility means when the enemy shoots a missile at it, one of a fighter's best tools to dodge a missile- evasive maneouvering - is not available to it.

All of this and more has been pointed out by various experts but there's a huge amount of money at stake here, and the shit most people hear in the media is just that money talking.

That's my understanding as well. While the air frame design is locked down, the specific F35 in this test was an early developmental model. This means it has early release flight software which will limit the available flight regime (lower angle of attack and and G limits - it can't turn as quickly), it also did not have the full radar and electronics wizardry available to the pilot. In short, it is not a representative example of the fighting capabilities of the production model. Having said that, I do think the programme has some very serious issues, and I'm not convinced it will deliver the bang per buck that has been promised.
